chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Fadl Abu al-Abbas, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
What is one of you doing by making a good deed apparent and concealing a bad one? Does he not reflect upon himself and realize that it is not so?
And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'But indeed, the human being is a witness against himself.'
Indeed, the inner self, when sound, strengthens the outward appearance.
Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Jamhur, from Fadalah, from Mu'awiya, from al-Fudayl, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) — similar to it.

key_terms.السَّرِيرَة: Inner self or secret state; the hidden reality of a person's character and intentions.
key_terms.الْعَلَانِيَة: Outward appearance or public display; the visible actions and deeds of a person.
key_terms.بَصِيرَة: Witness or evidence; referring to the self as a witness against itself on the Day of Judgment.

ai.seo_question: How does the inner self influence outward behavior in Shia ethics?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi critiques the hypocrisy of public piety by contrasting the 'sirati' (inner state) with 'alaniyah' (outward appearance), asserting that a purified heart naturally manifests in visible deeds. It underscores the Shia emphasis on 'ikhlas' (sincerity), where the internal reality of the self serves as the ultimate witness to one's true spiritual condition, as referenced in Surah Al-Qiyamah. The narration highlights that outward actions are merely the fruit of an inwardly sound soul, making inner integrity the prerequisite for authentic worship.
